solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Work to cross very strong river outside uni

indicators.note: a word set to cross something straddles it, so it ends up on either side of the other pieces

parts.note: an opus is a musical or literary work
fortissimo, the musical marking for very loud or strong
the river that flows through Cambridge

explanation.surface: A job building a bridge over a powerful river somewhere beyond the university grounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The work is split open after its first letter to take in the rest. The Cam flows through Cambridge, an apt river for a clue about a university.
explanation.definitionFit: Off-campus describes anything located or happening away from a university's premises.

clue.text: Concluded mob put too many pieces in a trunk?

definitions.text: put too many pieces in a trunk?

parts.note: something concluded is over
a pack is a crowd or mob

explanation.surface: A finished gang crammed too many items into a car boot or chest.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is an example: stuffing a trunk with too many items is one way to overpack.
explanation.definitionFit: To overpack is to fill luggage or a container beyond what it sensibly holds.

clue.text: Conservative in charge? Total shambles!

indicators.note: one item being in another means it sits inside that word's letters

parts.note: a fare is the charge for a journey
the standard abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A political jibe: the Tories running things means total chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In charge' reads as a single phrase meaning running things, but 'in' is the container signal and 'charge' is the fare.
explanation.definitionFit: A farce is a ridiculous, chaotic situation, a total shambles in the informal sense.

clue.text: Someone we've all sent a card to this Christmas?

definitions.text: Someone we've all sent a card to this Christmas?

parts.words: Someone we've all sent a card to this Christmas?
parts.note: surface reading: a friend everyone remembered with a Christmas card

parts.words: Someone we've all sent a card to
parts.note: setter's reading: anyone at all who receives a posted item, the generic term for the recipient

explanation.surface: Wondering about a popular person who received a card from everyone this festive season.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a particular friend, but every card recipient qualifies: the answer is simply the word for whoever a letter is directed to.
explanation.definitionFit: An addressee is the person to whom mail is directed, which describes anybody receiving our cards.

clue.text: Ghost ship finally getting a month at sea

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word it follows

parts.note: last letter of ship

indicators.note: at sea means confused and adrift, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A spectral vessel spends a month sailing the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ghost ship' looks like one phrase (as in the Flying Dutchman), but the definition is 'Ghost' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A phantom is an apparition or spirit, the same thing as a ghost.

clue.text: Trim small trees sold recently?

parts.note: spruce as an adjective means neat and trim
the standard abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A gardener's note about pruning the little saplings that just went on sale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trim small trees' reads as pruning, but 'Trim' is the adjective meaning neat. The question mark marks the definition as seasonal: spruces are the usual Christmas trees.
explanation.definitionFit: Spruces are the conifers most commonly bought as Christmas trees in the weeks before the holiday.

clue.text: Kids giving up time for posh birthday boy?

indicators.note: giving up one thing for another means a letter is surrendered and a replacement takes its place

parts.note: to kid is to joke or jest
T is the standard abbreviation for time
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U

explanation.surface: Children abandon their playtime for a smart party in honour of someone's birthday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kids' looks like children but is the verb, meaning teases. U for upper-class is a crossword staple from the 1950s U and non-U debate.
explanation.definitionFit: Christmas celebrates the nativity of Jesus, so in a Christmas puzzle he is the birthday boy.

clue.text: Area under no good biblical ruler where 6A lived

indicators.note: in a down answer, one piece under another follows it
with no good, the letter standing for good is taken out of the word

parts.note: the Judges were the rulers of Israel before its kings
G is the abbreviation for good
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A territory governed by a wicked Old Testament ruler, home of the 6 Across figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No good' looks like a description of the ruler's character; it actually removes a G. The answer refers back to 6 Across, Jesus.
explanation.definitionFit: Judea was the Roman province in southern Palestine where Jesus lived, preached and was crucified.

clue.text: Hoses down pants ready for a Lapland tramp?

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so these letters are in a poor, jumbled state

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sluices off their trousers before a long hike through Lapland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like trousers but is the British slang adjective for rubbish. The key prints SHOWSHOED; the letters only make SNOWSHOED.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone snowshoed has strapped on snowshoes, equipped for a long walk across Lapland's deep snow.

clue.text: Sort of cheeps that Phil's bird delivers today?

indicators.note: sort here is the verb, to arrange, so these letters are put in a different order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A query about the kind of chirping a pet bird belonging to someone called Phil makes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' is British slang for a woman: Prince Philip's wife was Queen Elizabeth II, whose Christmas Day broadcast is the Queen's Speech.
explanation.definitionFit: The monarch's televised Christmas Day address is known as the Queen's Speech, a speech delivered that day.

clue.text: Energy shown by a ginger with two listeners

parts.note: E is the symbol for energy
taken as written
ginger hair is red

explanation.surface: A lively redhead who is happy to hear both sides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Listeners' is a playful word for ears.
explanation.definitionFit: Eared means having ears, and listeners is a fanciful term for the ears themselves.

clue.text: Deer roam freely over old landing zone

indicators.note: roaming freely means wandering without fixed order, so these letters move about

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
O is the cricket abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Wild deer wander across a disused airfield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over old' tempts you to read 'old' as wordplay; 'over' gives O and 'old' belongs to the definition, since the word is dated.
explanation.definitionFit: Aerodrome is the old-fashioned term for a small airfield, a place where aircraft land.

clue.text: Here's something not seen under a tree every day

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in attendance, as in answering a register

definitions.text: something not seen under a tree every day
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a gift, found beneath the Christmas tree only once a year

explanation.surface: Offering someone an unusual item you would not normally find beneath a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here's' reads as 'here is'; the definition is 'Here', with the 's acting as the link 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Present means in attendance, and a present is a gift, laid beneath the Christmas tree only once a year.

clue.text: Enduring donkey dons get on … nearly

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
to don is to put on, so the second word wears the first like a garment

parts.note: to click is to get on well; nearly removes the K
an ass is a donkey

explanation.surface: A stubborn university fellow almost manages to get along with colleagues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' looks like university lecturers, but it is the verb, putting on. Note the container works backwards: the trimmed 'get on' word wraps around the donkey.
explanation.definitionFit: A classic is of lasting quality, enduring in value and appeal.

clue.text: Arch-moralists high on cold December air?

indicators.note: being high means intoxicated and disordered, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: Puritanical killjoys getting high on the chilly winter atmosphere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' looks like the atmosphere; it is a tune.
explanation.definitionFit: A Christmas carol is a festive song, and an air is a tune heard in December.

clue.text: One tweets "ruddy brute" about Republican leader

indicators.note: a leader is the opening letter, just one being taken here

parts.note: ruddy means red in colour

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: a beast is a brute
first letter of Republican

explanation.surface: A social-media post insulting a Republican party boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tweets' suggests social media; it is birdsong. Redbreast is the robin, the bird of British Christmas cards.
explanation.definitionFit: Redbreast is another name for the robin, a songbird that chirps or twitters.

clue.text: A large old queen drinking with a great man

indicators.note: drinking means taking something in, so one word swallows the other

parts.note: and means together with
L is the abbreviation for large
ex means former
taken as written
Elizabeth Regina, the royal cipher

explanation.surface: A very fat former queen sharing a drink with an eminent figure.
explanation.walkthrough: An old queen is an ex-queen, EX plus ER, which takes in AND. The definition points to Alexander the Great.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander the Great, the Macedonian conqueror, is history's best-known man given the epithet 'great'.

clue.text: Crazy types full of bad jokes at Yuletide?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: mad, in British slang

definitions.text: types full of bad jokes at Yuletide?
definitions.meaning: second meaning: Christmas novelties pulled to bang open, each holding a corny joke

explanation.surface: Mad folk who are overflowing with terrible festive humour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crazy types' reads as one phrase, but 'Crazy' is a definition on its own. A Christmas cracker is a paper tube pulled apart with a bang, containing a hat, a trinket and a groan-worthy joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Crackers is British slang for insane, and Christmas crackers famously contain feeble jokes.

clue.text: Mess vandal created around new countdown monitor?

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the single letter is enclosed in the jumble
a mess is a disorderly state, so these letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A hooligan has made a mess around some new display counting down the seconds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Monitor' suggests a screen; here it is something that keeps track of the days.
explanation.definitionFit: An advent calendar counts down the days of December to Christmas, opening one door each day.

clue.text: Colossal jerk seizing sunbed from Apple?

indicators.note: seizing means grabbing hold, so the outer word clasps the inner one

parts.note: a tic is an involuntary jerk
a joke Apple product name, like the iPod: the i prefix plus tan

explanation.surface: An idiot grabbing a tanning bed made by the tech company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' suggests an idiot, but it is a twitch. The setter invents an Apple gadget by putting Apple's lowercase i before a word for tanning.
explanation.definitionFit: Titanic means of gigantic size or strength, from the Titans of Greek myth.

clue.text: Some upstart is teasing a public performer …

indicators.note: some means a part of, so the answer is a portion of the words that follow

parts.note: the run of letters across these words

explanation.surface: A cheeky newcomer mocks an entertainer, continuing into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The trailing ellipsis just links the surface to 20 Down.
explanation.definitionFit: An artiste is a professional entertainer such as a singer or dancer who performs before an audience.

clue.text: … unhappy about this woman who's pulled Santa?

indicators.note: about means turned around, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: sad means unhappy
her refers to a woman

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: a miserable woman who has managed to seduce Father Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulled' in British slang means attracted romantically, which the surface plays on; the definition means drew the sleigh.
explanation.definitionFit: Dasher is one of Santa's reindeer, named first in 'A Visit from St Nicholas', who haul his sleigh.

clue.text: Tumbler a Slav filled with drop of brandy

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: filled with means containing, so the next item goes inside

parts.note: a Croat is a Slav from Croatia

indicators.note: just a drop of a drink means only its first bit is used

parts.note: first letter of brandy

explanation.surface: A glass belonging to an Eastern European, topped up with a splash of cognac.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tumbler' looks like a drinking glass, matching the brandy, but it is a gymnast.
explanation.definitionFit: A tumbler is a performer of somersaults and handsprings, an acrobat.

clue.text: Those ringing in the New Year with a Scotch?

definitions.text: Those ringing in the New Year
definitions.meaning: first meaning: church chimes that peal at midnight
second meaning: a well-known brand of blended Scotch whisky

explanation.surface: People welcoming in January with a dram of whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: Bell's is a popular brand of blended Scotch whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: Church chimes peal out the New Year, and Bell's is a blended Scotch whisky brand.

clue.text: Illicit trade that's seen by the roadside?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: dealing in something illegal, such as drugs
second meaning: vehicles watched from the side of the road

explanation.surface: Black-market dealing that goes on openly beside a highway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Illicit trade' needs the specific sense of trafficking, as in drug traffic.
explanation.definitionFit: Traffic is illegal dealing in goods, and the stream of vehicles passing along the road.

clue.text: Celebrity welcoming Liberal sweetheart

indicators.note: welcoming means taking someone in, so one word holds the other

parts.note: fame is celebrity, the state of being well known
the standard abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A famous person greets a Lib Dem politician they are romantically involved with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Celebrity' reads as a famous person, but here it is the abstract noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A flame is a lover or sweetheart, as in the phrase an old flame.

clue.text: Newspaper features linked with furrowed brows?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the large titles above stories
second meaning, read whimsically: creases on the forehead

explanation.surface: Front-page stories that make readers frown.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the second sense as a pun: a furrowed brow has lines on the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Headlines top newspaper stories, and taken literally the word means lines on one's head, wrinkles.

clue.text: Daughter with garden tool? Duck!

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter
a rake is a garden implement

explanation.surface: A girl swings a gardening implement and someone shouts a warning to get down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck!' looks like a shouted warning, but it is the noun: a drake is a male duck.
explanation.definitionFit: A drake is a male duck, an example of the bird.

clue.text: Decline when they tell us when to work

definitions.text: they tell us when to work

parts.note: to rot is to decay or decline
as can mean when, as in 'as I arrived'

explanation.surface: Turning down shifts when the schedules arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decline' suggests refusing; it means decay.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotas are duty schedules listing who works which shift.

clue.text: Gloomy match-goer with sore throat apt do this?

definitions.text: match-goer with sore throat apt do this?
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read as two words: a fan with a sore throat would shout less

explanation.surface: A miserable sports fan with a croaky throat, likely to stay quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half splits the answer into two words, cheer less. The clue reads 'apt do', apparently a slip for 'apt to do'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheerless means gloomy and dismal, lacking any brightness or joy.
